nature-res-211.title: Is nuclear fuel renewable?
nature-res-211.text: Mined uranium is finite, yet some reactors make more fuel than they burn. That puzzle drives a debate over whether nuclear fuels should count as renewable. In 1987 the World Commission on Environment and Development classed breeder reactors, which produce more fissile fuel than they consume, as renewable sources of energy. Uranium, the most common fission fuel, occurs at low concentrations and is mined in 19 countries. Nuclear power provides about 6% of the world's energy and 13–14% of its electricity. Its plants also produce about 10,000 metric tons of high level waste a year, hazardous if not properly contained.

nature-res-250.title: Resource wars: fighting over what lies in the ground
nature-res-250.text: In the 19th century, nations fought over bird droppings: guano, a nutrient-rich fertilizer, piled on Peru's Chincha Islands. A resource war is a war caused by conflict over resources, typically between whoever controls a resource and an aggressor who wants it. Industrialization raised the raw materials nations need, and such power struggles have underlain conflicts since the late 19th century. Two views compete. The geopolitical view sees resource conflict as strategic; the environmental security view sees it as a response to scarcity. Fights can also center on control of resource revenues.

nature-res-238.title: Grading mineral deposits by confidence and profit
nature-res-238.text: Not every deposit in the ground counts as a reserve. A mineral resource is material in or on the Earth's crust with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. In increasing geological confidence, resources are inferred, indicated or measured. A mineral reserve is the part of a measured or indicated resource that can be mined at a profit, split into probable and, with highest confidence, proved reserves. Most schemes follow the CRIRSCO International Reporting Template, such as Australia's JORC Code; the UN Framework Classification for Resources dates from 1997. Because ores are concentrated unevenly, extraction eventually meets diminishing returns as it moves to poorer, less accessible sites.

nature-res-235.title: Malthus's two brakes on population
nature-res-235.text: Malthus saw two kinds of brake on population. Preventive checks lower birth rates, through celibacy and chastity. Positive checks shorten lives: chiefly war, plague and famine, but also poor health and economic conditions. When positive checks cause high rates of premature death, the result is called a Malthusian catastrophe.

nature-res-236.title: Neo-Malthusianism: the old fear in modern form
nature-res-236.text: After the Second World War, crop gains were followed by rapid growth in human numbers. Paul R. Ehrlich and others then predicted an imminent Malthusian catastrophe. Neo-Malthusianism is the concern that too many people consuming too much will exhaust resources. The fear is that the environment then degrades until ecosystems collapse. {{ref:nature-hist-040}} and Jeremy Rifkin raised such concerns about modern mechanized farming. The emphasis has shifted, though. A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that sustainability worries had moved from the number of people to the balance between consumption and saving.

nature-res-219.title: Quasi-rent: a machine's temporary windfall
nature-res-219.text: Rent is not only for land. Alfred Marshall extended the idea to machines, buildings and other durable man-made factors whose supply is fixed for the time being. Quasi-rent is the short-run, rent-like return such a factor earns. Unlike pure rent, it rewards the action needed to earn it. And it does not last: in the long run it is competed away as new capital enters.

nature-res-224.title: Proven, probable, possible: counting oil reserves
nature-res-224.text: Oil companies sort reserves by how likely they are to be produced. Proven, or 1P, reserves have at least a 90% probability of production. Proven plus probable, 2P, have at least 50%, and proven, probable and possible, 3P, at least 10%. Conventional and unconventional reserves are counted separately. Critics say stated world reserves are inflated, with many so-called reserves actually being resources not available for production.

nature-res-223.title: Peak oil demand: when people stop wanting more
nature-res-223.text: Oil use might peak before oil runs short. Peak oil demand is the idea that world consumption will top out because people deliberately cut it. The International Energy Agency argues demand will be cut first, to address climate change and greenhouse gas emissions. The idea relies on electric vehicles and possibly biofuels replacing gasoline and diesel vehicles. Road transport is the obvious target: it takes about 50% of oil use in OECD countries.

nature-res-225.title: Unconventional oil: the hard-to-get barrels
nature-res-225.text: Oil sands are oil, but getting the oil out takes many processing steps, which makes production costs extremely high. Unconventional oil is oil that is difficult to extract, as opposed to conventional oil from easy onshore and shallow offshore fields. As conventional oil grows scarcer, liquids from tight oil, oil sands, oil shale, gas-to-liquids, coal-to-liquids and biofuels can replace it.

nature-res-203.title: The aid curse: when help weakens government
nature-res-203.text: Foreign aid can resemble an oil field in one troubling way. The aid curse is the argument that heavy reliance on aid can harm a country's development in the long run, much like the resource curse. Like resource revenue, aid is unearned income. It can weaken politicians' accountability to citizens and reduce pressure to reform. When aid is a major source of government revenue, rulers have less reason to build a tax system and answer to taxpayers.

nature-res-202.title: Petro-aggression: oil states and war
nature-res-202.text: Petrostates, countries that get 10% or more of their GDP from petroleum, are 250 percent more likely to start international conflicts than a typical country. That was Jeff Colgan's finding in a 2013 book that popularized the term petro-aggression: the tendency of a petrostate to start international conflicts or to be their target. Whether the same pattern holds for resources other than oil remains unclear.

nature-res-201.title: Boom and bust in the national budget
nature-res-201.text: Between 1998 and 2008, crude oil rose from $10 a barrel to $145, then fell by more than half, to $60, in a few months. Governments that depend on such resources face large, sudden swings in their income. Some depend almost entirely: in 2005, 99.3% of Angola's exports came from oil and diamonds alone. Abrupt revenue changes often lead to broken contracts or cuts to social programs, eroding the rule of law and public support.

nature-res-243.title: Sovereign wealth funds: saving the windfall
nature-res-243.text: In 1953 Kuwait set up the first sovereign wealth fund for a state, the Kuwait Investment Authority, using oil revenues. A sovereign wealth fund is a state-owned investment fund that buys assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate and precious metals. Most are funded by commodity export revenues or by central bank foreign currency reserves, and many were set up by oil-rich states. For commodity exporters, a fund can smooth volatile government revenue and save for the longer term. Assets under management reached $13–15 trillion by 2025; funds built on oil and gas exports held $5.4 trillion as of 2020. In 2008 the IMF led the drafting of the 24 Santiago Principles, standards for transparency, independence and accountability. Many funds have still been exhausted, mainly through political instability rather than economic factors.

nature-res-241.title: Severance taxes: charging for what is taken out
nature-res-241.text: As of 2021, 34 US states collected a severance tax on oil and gas. It is a tax charged on removing natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, uranium or timber within a taxing jurisdiction. It is used where resources are privately owned, as in the United States. Where the public owns them, a resource royalty is paid instead, called stumpage for timber. Some states put the revenue into permanent endowments meant to outlast extraction, from about $800 million in Montana to more than $37 billion in Alaska. Severance taxes count among environmental taxes and are cited as classic Pigouvian taxes.

nature-res-215.title: Perpetual resources: too plentiful to run out
nature-res-215.text: In 1900 the average copper ore processed held 4.0% copper; by 2000 it held just 0.44%. Better recovery keeps lowering the grade worth mining. A perpetual resource is one so large relative to demand that it is unlikely ever to run out on a human time scale. Salt, stone, magnesium and common clay qualify, and new technology added synthetic diamonds to the list. The status shifts with technology, needs and prices, with how recyclable a material is, and with whether substitutes exist. Julian Simon went furthest, claiming the supply of natural resources is infinite, that is, perpetual.

nature-res-216.title: Paleoresources: plenty that nobody wants
nature-res-216.text: Arrowhead-grade flint is still out there, but nobody needs it now that sharpened scrap steel is simpler. A paleoresource is a resource with little or no demand left because its material has gone out of use. US anthracite coal shows how it happens. Production fell from 70.4 million tonnes in 1905 to 1.5 million tonnes in 2005, so its reserves are now more than perpetual. Decline feeds itself: as customers switch fuels, dealers and then mines lose too much sales volume to cover costs, and close.

nature-res-246.title: Blue finance: money for healthier oceans
nature-res-246.text: The World Economic Forum estimates that meeting SDG 14, the UN goal for the oceans, needs US$175 billion a year. It is the most underfunded of all 17 goals. Blue finance is finance that cuts the carbon footprint of ocean-related activities and benefits the marine environment. It is part of {{ref:nature-mkt-018}} and overlaps with funding for climate action. It pays for offshore wind and other marine renewable energy, zero-emission shipping, and the restoration of mangroves and seagrass meadows.

nature-res-247.title: Blue justice: who loses when the sea is developed
nature-res-247.text: Some coastal communities have fished the same waters for thousands of years. Blue justice is a critical approach that asks how blue economy and blue growth initiatives affect such communities and their small-scale fisheries. It recognizes their historical rights to marine resources and coastal space. It also studies the pressures these fisheries face from industrial fishing, tourism, fish farming and energy production.

nature-res-251.title: Conflict resources: commodities that pay for war
nature-res-251.text: In the late 1990s, 'blood diamonds' financed rebellions in Angola and Sierra Leone. 'Conflict timber' followed, in Cambodia and Liberia. Conflict resources are natural resources extracted in a conflict zone and sold to keep the fighting going. Statistical and anecdotal evidence suggests precious commodities can prolong conflicts. The US, EU and OECD now treat tantalum, tin, tungsten and gold from conflict in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as conflict minerals. They require companies to report their use.

nature-res-230.title: The Corden–Neary model of Dutch disease
nature-res-230.text: The classic 1982 model of Dutch disease splits an economy in three: a booming sector, a lagging sector that trades abroad, and a services sector that does not. The boom hurts the lagging sector two ways. In the resource movement effect, the boom pulls workers into the booming sector, called direct deindustrialization. In the spending effect, extra revenue raises demand for services, pulling workers from the lagging sector and raising the real exchange rate. The spending effect is usually seen as the main channel, because extraction relies on machinery and employs few workers.

nature-res-252.title: Hotelling rent: the value of leaving some for later
nature-res-252.text: A barrel pumped today is a barrel nobody can pump tomorrow, and that loss has a price. Hotelling rent, also called scarcity or depletion rent, is the extra value a finite resource earns for exactly this reason. It is the maximum rent obtainable while emptying the stock. Under Hotelling's rule it rises each year at the rate of interest. If today's price were lower, a producer would rather extract less now and more later. Scarcity rents also help explain why the best tax on a pollutant from a finite fuel can be lower than the pollutant's marginal damages.

nature-res-254.title: Measuring scarcity through prices
nature-res-254.text: How can anyone tell whether resources are running out? Resource scarcity indicators are measures, such as a resource's inflation-adjusted price, used to judge it. Total stocks and future markets are unknown, so most economists do not trust physical quantities as a guide. An alternative measures a resource's usable quantity through its price and opportunity cost. The Simon–Ehrlich wager used the inflation-adjusted prices of five metals as its agreed yardstick. From 2005 through 2013, real prices of energy and metals stayed well above their long-term averages.

nature-res-217.title: Resource substitution: escaping a shortage
nature-res-217.text: Tin foil became aluminum foil because tin grew scarce. Resource substitution means replacing a scarce material with another in its end uses, a main way economies escape shortages. Tin-plated cans gave way to polymer-lined steel cans and aseptic packaging too. When a 1978 invasion disrupted cobalt supply and briefly tripled its price, nickel and other substitutes stepped in. Most mineral resources can be stretched by {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} and by substitutes for the products made from them, which shapes demand for minerals and so their availability.

nature-res-228.title: Critical raw materials: few suppliers, no substitutes
nature-res-228.text: In 2023 Europe relied on China for 98% of its rare-earth needs and 97% of its lithium. Critical raw materials have no viable substitutes with current technology, must be imported by most consuming countries, and are supplied mainly by one or a few producers. The European Commission's list grew from 14 materials in 2011 to 34 in 2023, mainly for clean energy and digital technologies. Its Critical Raw Materials Act came into force on 23 May 2024. By 2030 the EU aims to extract at least 10%, process at least 40% and recycle at least 25% of its yearly consumption at home.

nature-res-253.title: Stock effects: why extraction gets harder
nature-res-253.text: The easy ore goes first. Stock effects are the tendency for extraction to become costlier as a resource stock is drawn down, pushing producers to less accessible sites and lower-grade ores. Because ores are concentrated unevenly, mining eventually meets diminishing returns, and extraction costs tend to rise over time. Falling average ore grades mean deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock. Even with constant extraction costs, a resource's value rises as it grows scarcer.

nature-res-206.title: Peak minerals: mining after the easy ore
nature-res-206.text: A region's mining history splits at its peak. Before it, ores are cheap and easy to reach; after it, they cost more. Peak minerals is a model of how mining's costs and impacts change as ore quality declines around that peak. Falling average ore grades are the key sign that production is getting more expensive, bringing deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock. Running out is another matter. Unlike coal, oil or phosphorus, most non-energy minerals and metals are unlikely to be exhausted.

nature-res-226.title: Backstop resources: alternatives that wait for high prices
nature-res-226.text: After the 1979 oil price spike, Canada developed its tar sands. Under anti-apartheid embargoes, South Africa turned coal into fuel. Both fit the backstop theory: as a heavily used limited resource grows expensive, alternatives become cheap by comparison and worth using. In the long run, the theory assumes need will drive technology until backstop resources are essentially unlimited. Environmental economists dispute that faith in technology. Critics say it ignores the infrastructure alternatives need: a hydrogen car is easy compared with building a network to supply hydrogen.

nature-res-240.title: Resource rent tax: sharing the surplus
nature-res-240.text: A resource rent tax charges nothing until a project earns a set rate of return. After that, the government shares in the profits. It taxes the rent, the surplus beyond the necessary costs of production, including a reward to capital, and can apply to renewable and non-renewable resources alike. It is most common in mining and petroleum. Norway has also applied it to fish farming from 2023 and onshore wind from 2024, Iceland to fishing and Switzerland to hydropower.

reviews.renewable-and-non-renewable-resources: Every man-made product starts as a natural resource, and the key divide is between resources that regrow and those that can be extracted only once. Using either faster than it is replaced is depletion, a fear as old as Malthus and as fresh as forecasts of peak oil and the Simon–Ehrlich wager over metal prices. Economists watch the money as well as the stock: scarce, unevenly spread land, oil and ore earn rent, and Hotelling showed why a finite resource's net price should rise over time. Those rents can curse as well as bless, through swinging revenues, Dutch disease and conflict. Sovereign wealth funds, severance taxes and resource rent taxes are the tools governments use to turn a passing windfall into lasting wealth.
